content.thinking:
I should avoid writing specific figures myself and stick to placeholders. Looking at the symptoms, the HighLatency alert fired with slow account pages and failed requests, while error rate stayed nearly flat—just a small rise from baseline to peak. I'm starting to trace the causal chain from the user-facing symptom of slow pages toward whatever change triggered it.

Tracing further, latency spiked when autoscaler capacity dropped back down while CPU usage stayed elevated, then the autoscaler kept flapping between a low and high capacity level instead of settling, even as demand plateaued. The evidence stops once traffic climbed several-fold with no corresponding change events logged. I'm treating the root cause as capacity oscillation with too low a floor given rising traffic, and the fix as roughly doubling that floor level—being careful to describe this without citing exact numbers, just "the lower capacity level" versus "a higher floor." I'm also checking the citation labels for confirmation status and noting that recovery in the metrics appears to happen before the mitigation was actually applied, which is worth flagging as a timing inconsistency.

Looking at detection gaps too: the alert fired after the metrics had already recovered, meaning detection lagged behind the actual fix. Also noting a naming mismatch—the alert was labeled for error rate but the underlying series was actually latency. I'm drafting action items around these gaps: alerting on autoscaler flapping, reviewing scale-down stabilization settings, and fixing the alert timing/labeling issue, numbering them as follow-on tasks. I want the executive summary to reference duration generically and avoid dropping in other specific numbers.

action_items.item: Review the autoscaler's scale-down settings for io-shop, such as stabilization window and CPU target. It should not reclaim capacity while CPU use is at or above the lower limit. Then confirm the raised minimum capacity is still the right size for the new traffic level.
Add an alert on autoscaler flapping for io-shop: capacity limit changing direction repeatedly within a short window while request volume is steady.
Fix the HighLatency alert so its description matches the series it evaluates (latency, not error rate). Review its evaluation delay so it pages while the fault is still happening.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers saw slow account pages. Some disconnected before the page loaded, and the error rate rose only slightly. The latency series behind the alert rose far above its earlier level, from {series_before} to {series_while_broken} on average and {series_at_worst} at worst.

Latency spiked each time the service's CPU limit fell back to its lower level while CPU use was already at or above that level. Latency partly recovered when the limit went back up. The service was repeatedly short of capacity.

The autoscaler flapped between the low and high capacity levels every minute or two. It kept doing so after request volume stopped climbing and held a steady plateau, so it was not settling on a size.

Traffic had risen several-fold over a short period, which started the scaling activity. The service's normal capacity was below what the new load needed, so each scale-down put it in deficit. No deploy, release or flag change preceded this, so the load was the trigger and not a change.
Raising the autoscaler's minimum capacity stopped the drops to the low level. The service returned to baseline and the paging rule stopped firing.

contributing_factors.factor: The autoscaler's scale-down behaviour had no damping against traffic that stayed high. It could reclaim capacity while CPU use was still at or above the lower limit. The draft fix is still open and the minimum-capacity raise is only a stopgap.
Nothing detected autoscaler flapping, so repeated capacity oscillation went unnoticed while traffic had been elevated for a long time before the page.

The page arrived after the metrics already showed recovery. The alert text named an error rate, but the series it evaluates is latency, and the error rate hardly moved. This delayed and confused the response.

input.executive_summary: For about {duration}, from {began} to {recovered}, shoppers using io-shop's account pages got slow responses. Some gave up and disconnected. The error rate barely moved: it was {errors_before} before and {errors_while_broken} during, peaking at {errors_at_worst}. The cause was the service's capacity controller, which kept adding and then removing capacity while traffic was high and steady. Argus raised the minimum capacity so the service could not drop back to the lower level. The service was confirmed back at baseline and the incident closed at {closed}. A draft fix is open for review. The metrics show recovery before the mitigation was applied, so the mitigation's effect is not fully proven.

got_lucky: The impact was short and the error rate hardly rose, because slow responses did not turn into widespread failures.
The oscillation could have gone on if traffic had stayed high. The recovery may have come from the oscillation easing by itself, which means the same flapping could return.
went_well: Argus read metrics, logs, changes and flag history quickly and ruled out deploys and flag changes.
The leading candidate was acted on straight away with a reversible, low-risk change, and its result was checked before closing.
A draft fix pull request was proposed.
went_wrong: The page came after the metrics showed recovery, and the alert text described an error rate while the paged series was latency.
The autoscaler oscillation lasted a long time before anything flagged it.
The mitigation was applied after the metrics showed recovery, so the evidence that it fixed the problem is weak.

input.root_cause: io-shop's autoscaler would not settle. After traffic rose several-fold and then plateaued, it kept switching capacity between a low and a high level. Each time it dropped back to the low level, CPU demand was at or above that capacity and latency spiked.
